big: Meena's bond fund is down 4% this month. Nobody defaulted. No company failed. So what pulled the price down?

lines: My debt fund fell, but no borrower defaulted. How can that happen?
Because bond prices move with interest rates. Let us watch a ₹100 bond paying 7% when market rates change by 1%.

alt: Two sets of bars showing how a short bond and a long bond move when market rates rise or fall
caps: A ₹100 bond pays 7%. Market rates now move by 1%.
If rates rise to 8%, the 10-year bond drops to about ₹93. The 1-year barely moves.
If rates fall to 6%, the 10-year bond rises to about ₹107.
Longer bonds swing more. That sensitivity is called duration.

intro: Prices rise every year, so what you earn must be compared with that.
note: This is the real return: what your interest earns after taking away rising prices.

q: Market interest rates rise. What usually happens to the price of a bond you already hold?
opts: It rises, because higher rates make every existing bond more valuable
It stays the same, since a bond's price is fixed once it is issued
It doubles, since the coupon is automatically raised to match the rise
It falls, because new bonds pay more and yours becomes less attractive
why: Rising rates do the opposite. Older, lower-rate bonds are worth less when new ones pay more.
A bond's price can change in the market. Only its coupon and face value are fixed.
A coupon never changes once set. Nothing about a rate rise adjusts it upward.
New bonds pay higher rates, so buyers pay less for your lower-rate bond, and its price falls.

q: Rates rise by 1%. Fund A holds bonds ending in one year, and Fund B holds bonds ending in twenty years. What is likely?
opts: Both fall by the same amount, since the rate rise is the same for each
Fund B falls more, since longer duration means bigger price swings
Fund A falls more, because short bonds are the most exposed to rates
Neither falls, since bond funds are protected from rate changes
why: The same rate change hits bonds differently depending on how long they run.
Longer-dated bonds are more sensitive, so Fund B swings by more than Fund A.
Short bonds are the least sensitive, since they end soon and can be reinvested at new rates.
Bond funds are not protected. Rising rates can lower their value, as in this example.

q: A deposit pays 7% a year while prices rise 6% a year. What is the real return, roughly?
opts: About 13%, since interest and inflation are added together
About 7%, because inflation affects only the cost of goods
About 1%, so buying power grows only slightly
About 6%, because inflation is the main part of the earnings
why: Inflation reduces what money buys. It is taken away from the return, not added to it.
Inflation does reduce what your interest can buy, so the real gain is lower than 7%.
Seven percent minus six percent leaves about one percent of real growth in buying power.
Inflation is not part of the earnings. It is the loss in buying power that you must subtract.

q: A ₹100 bond with an 8% coupon is bought for ₹95. How does the yield compare with 8%?
opts: Higher, since ₹8 a year and a ₹100 repayment on ₹95 earns more
Lower, because paying less than face value reduces the earnings
Exactly 8%, since the coupon always equals the yield
Zero, since a bond bought below face value pays no interest
why: You pay ₹95 and receive ₹8 a year plus ₹100 at the end, so you earn more than 8% on your money.
Paying less than face value for the same payments raises the return, not lowers it.
Yield equals the coupon only when the price equals the face value. Here it does not.
A bond pays its coupon whatever price the buyer paid. The interest does not disappear.

pts: Bond prices and market interest rates move in opposite directions.
Longer duration means bigger swings when rates change.
Judge returns after inflation, since that is what you can actually buy.
